detailed_summary: The paper calculates nonlocal fluctuation corrections to the conductivity tensor within time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory and maps them to NV relaxometry observables. For single NV centers it predicts how relaxation depends on temperature, standoff distance, and probe frequency near Tc. For two-sensor covariance magnetometry it shows that field correlators acquire spatial structure set by the superconducting fluctuation correlation length, including nonequilibrium anisotropy under dc bias.
platform_or_system: NV-center noise magnetometry of superconducting films
main_result: The analysis predicts measurable single- and two-sensor magnetic-noise signatures of nonlocal superconducting fluctuations and biased nonequilibrium current noise.
application_angle: It gives scanning quantum sensors a concrete route to probe critical superconducting dynamics and transport noise beyond local conductivity measurements.

title: Fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing with a single nucleus per node
abstract: Distributed quantum computing interconnects small, high-quality nodes through optical links, but this architecture carries a pronounced asymmetry: in-node gates and measurements are cheap and high-fidelity, whereas inter-node communication relies on a low-coherence communication qubit and faulty photonics. Previous approaches overcame the noisy link by placing several high-quality data qubits in each node and consuming them for Bell pair and GHZ state distillation. Here we show that distillation can be avoided altogether. The key observation is that we can engineer a communication error bias, where photonic Bell pairs suffer frequent phase errors but only rare bit-flip errors. We design the syndrome-extraction circuits so that this phase noise appears solely as a measurement error that does not propagate to the data qubits, and is therefore suppressed by simply repeating the measurement; letting the error-correcting code itself, rather than a dedicated distillation subroutine, to purify the link. This dramatically reduces the need for ancillary nuclei: Floquet codes require only a single data qubit per node, while general stabilizer codes require just one additional ancilla. We demonstrate high error-correction thresholds throughout this regime, and we identify lattice surgery as inherently robust for this setting, enabling logical operations at a threshold close to that of quantum memory. As a result, the performance of the quantum computer is limited by the high-quality data qubits, while the requirements on photon indistinguishability and coherence of the communication qubit are substantially relaxed.
one_liner: Proposes fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing using only one long-lived nuclear data qubit per node.
why_it_matters: Avoiding link distillation sharply reduces node complexity while relaxing photonic indistinguishability and communication-qubit coherence requirements.
detailed_summary: The paper exploits engineered communication error bias so noisy photonic Bell-pair phase errors enter syndrome extraction as repeatable measurement errors rather than data errors. This lets the error-correcting code purify the inter-node link without separate Bell-pair or GHZ distillation. Floquet-code constructions need only a single data qubit per node, while general stabilizer codes require one extra ancilla, with high thresholds across the targeted regime.
platform_or_system: spin nodes linked by biased photonic Bell pairs
main_result: The authors show that distributed fault tolerance can be achieved without explicit link distillation and with as little as one nuclear data qubit per node.
application_angle: The scheme lowers hardware overhead for modular quantum computers and eases optical-link specifications for scalable networked processors.

title: Resolving Structure in Prethermal Floquet Dynamics with Precision Quantum Computation
abstract: Periodically driven interacting quantum many-body systems can exhibit long-lived prethermal dynamics, where local observables retain coherent structure even as entanglement and operator complexity grow. Accessing this regime at the system sizes and times needed to determine physical properties of the prethermal state remains a central challenge: state-of-the-art classical methods become unreliable, while noise in quantum hardware degrades observable expectation values. Here we overcome these limitations for a Floquet Ising magnet realized on a heavy-hex lattice. Using the advanced error mitigation software QESEM on an IBM Heron r3 superconducting quantum processor, we measure magnetization dynamics with percent-level precision and resolve long-lived subharmonic prethermal oscillations in systems of up to 74 qubits. These experiments reach regimes for which leading tensor-network simulations fail to converge, while sparse Pauli-path simulations remain strongly truncation dependent despite extensive computations on advanced GPUs and the Fugaku supercomputer. Leveraging this quantum-accessible regime, we extend finite-size scaling to larger systems and find an unexpectedly slow decrease of the oscillation amplitude with system size, providing strong evidence that this oscillatory response persists in the thermodynamic limit of heavy-hex ladders. A hierarchy of mitigation and validation tests, including unbiased error mitigation, agreement between independent mitigation estimators, noise-model validation on the superconducting hardware, and cross-platform corroboration at selected Floquet cycles on Quantinuum System Model H2 and Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion hardware, supports the reliability of these findings. Our work establishes error-mitigated quantum processors as quantitative scientific instruments for discovering new physics in non-equilibrium quantum matter.
one_liner: Uses error-mitigated IBM Heron hardware to resolve prethermal Floquet oscillations in heavy-hex Ising systems up to 74 qubits.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates quantum processors producing quantitative many-body physics data beyond converged tensor-network simulations.
detailed_summary: The study measures magnetization dynamics of a periodically driven Floquet Ising magnet on an IBM Heron r3 superconducting processor using QESEM error mitigation. It resolves long-lived subharmonic prethermal oscillations in systems up to 74 qubits, a regime where tensor-network simulations fail to converge and Pauli-path methods remain truncation sensitive. Cross-checks include independent mitigation estimators, noise-model validation, and selected corroboration on Quantinuum trapped-ion systems.
main_result: Error-mitigated measurements achieved percent-level precision and supported persistence of heavy-hex ladder prethermal oscillations toward the thermodynamic limit.
application_angle: The result strengthens the case for near-term quantum processors as scientific instruments for non-equilibrium quantum matter.

title: Numerical Modeling of Quasiparticle-Induced Dissipation in Fluxonium Qubits
abstract: Nonequilibrium quasiparticles (QPs) generated by stray infrared and ionizing radiation can limit the performance of superconducting quantum processors and present challenges for quantum error correction schemes. Models of QP-induced energy relaxation commonly assume that the characteristic energy of the QPs and the qubit transition energy are both small relative to the superconducting gap. Under these assumptions, certain qubits such as the fluxonium would exhibit protection against QP-induced dissipation at specific bias points. Here, we show that this is not necessarily the case, numerically analyzing the predicted rate of QP-induced dissipation in fluxonium qubits for different QP energy distributions and for QPs created via photon-assisted tunneling processes. We find that accounting for small numerical factors, existing theoretical models predict sensitivity to QP-induced errors at bias points previously thought to be protected. We find that inclusion of asymmetry in the superconducting gap energy across the junction can reintroduce suppression of QP-induced relaxation, as expected. Additionally, for QPs created by photon-assisted tunneling, we predict that $T_1$ protection will only occur for a specific energy of pair-breaking radiation. This understanding of fluxonium sensitivity to QP-induced dissipation informs the development of fluxonium-based processors and future QP-mitigation strategies.
one_liner: Numerically revisits quasiparticle-induced relaxation in fluxonium and finds protected bias points can remain sensitive.
why_it_matters: More realistic quasiparticle energy and junction-gap modeling changes expectations for fluxonium T1 protection and mitigation design.
detailed_summary: The paper numerically models quasiparticle-induced dissipation in fluxonium beyond common approximations that assume quasiparticle and transition energies are small relative to the superconducting gap. It finds that small numerical factors in existing models can make nominally protected bias points sensitive to quasiparticle errors. Gap asymmetry can restore suppression, while photon-assisted tunneling gives T1 protection only for a specific pair-breaking radiation energy.
main_result: The modeling shows that quasiparticle-induced relaxation can persist at fluxonium bias points previously expected to be protected unless device asymmetry or radiation energy conditions intervene.
application_angle: The findings guide fluxonium processor design, radiation shielding, and quasiparticle mitigation for more reliable superconducting quantum hardware.

title: Realizing Error Suppression in Partially Fault-Tolerant Quantum Simulations with IBM Quantum Computers
abstract: Quantum error-detecting codes offer a near-term path for improving the performance of quantum simulations on noisy hardware. Using IBM's superconducting quantum computer ibm_boston, we show that partially fault-tolerant encoded quantum simulations of the Ising model in 1+1D and 2+1D outperform their unencoded counterparts in estimating local observables. To represent 42 logical qubits on the heavy-hex quantum processor, 21 blocks of the [[4, 2, 2]] Iceberg code and up to 136 physical qubits are used. By pairing fault-tolerant syndrome extraction with non-fault-tolerant logical operations, this scheme preserves many of the benefits of error detection while avoiding the overhead typically required for a fully fault-tolerant logical gate set. The encoding's square logical connectivity, together with the freedom to place logical qubits within each block, enables simulations of a 2D spatial lattice with lower circuit depth than the unencoded implementation requires. We introduce Observable-Ranked Postselection, a selective-filtering technique based on syndrome correlations that recovers reliable results without the prohibitive shot loss of full syndrome postselection. Under the cumulative effect of device errors, this encoding improves local-observable accuracy over the unencoded baseline by 2-6% at intermediate times in 1+1D simulations, growing with circuit depth to over 200% in 2+1D at the latest times studied.
one_liner: Demonstrates encoded Ising simulations on IBM hardware where partial fault tolerance beats unencoded local-observable estimates.
why_it_matters: It shows error-detecting codes can improve useful near-term quantum simulations without full fault-tolerant logical gates.
detailed_summary: The work implements encoded quantum simulations of 1+1D and 2+1D Ising models on IBM's heavy-hex superconducting hardware using 21 blocks of the [[4,2,2]] Iceberg code. It combines fault-tolerant syndrome extraction with non-fault-tolerant logical operations, preserving some detection benefits while limiting overhead. Observable-Ranked Postselection uses syndrome correlations to improve estimates without the severe shot loss of full postselection.
main_result: Encoded partially fault-tolerant simulations improved local-observable accuracy over unencoded baselines, reaching over 200% improvement at late times in 2+1D cases.
application_angle: The approach offers a practical near-term path to more accurate lattice and many-body simulations on noisy superconducting processors.

title: Spin-cQED with bulk germanium spin qubits
abstract: Unstrained bulk germanium is a particularly attractive material for circuit quantum electrodynamics with spins (spin-cQED). We show, through systematic modeling and comparison with state-of-the-art strained germanium heterostructures, that hole spins in bulk germanium double quantum dots readily reach the strong-coupling regime with superconducting microwave resonators, achieving spin-photon coupling strengths $g_s/2π\gtrsim100$\,MHz. This enhancement originates from large spin-orbit interactions beyond the perturbative regime. In addition, the coupling is much less sensitive to the orientation of the applied magnetic field, which shall ease operation and limit the impact of device-to-device variability. Our results establish bulk germanium as a compelling platform for scalable spin-cQED.
one_liner: Modeling predicts strong spin-photon coupling for hole spins in bulk Ge double quantum dots coupled to microwave resonators.
why_it_matters: Bulk Ge could simplify scalable spin-cQED by delivering >100 MHz coupling with reduced magnetic-field-orientation sensitivity.
detailed_summary: The paper models hole-spin qubits in unstrained bulk germanium double quantum dots coupled to superconducting microwave resonators. It predicts spin-photon coupling strengths gs/2pi above about 100 MHz, driven by strong nonperturbative spin-orbit interactions. Compared with strained Ge heterostructures, the coupling is less sensitive to magnetic-field orientation, which may ease calibration and reduce device variability.
platform_or_system: bulk Ge hole-spin double quantum dots
main_result: Bulk Ge spin qubits are predicted to readily reach the strong-coupling spin-cQED regime with superconducting resonators.
application_angle: The result points to a more robust materials platform for scalable semiconductor spin-qubit processors with microwave interconnects.

title: Universal Optimization and Tighter Fidelity Bounds for Approximate Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Approximate quantum error correction (AQEC) not only dictates the performance of discrete- and continuous-variable quantum error correction codes but also serves as a unifying framework across various physical disciplines. Identifying the optimal recovery channel to maximize the entanglement fidelity via standard semidefinite programming is computationally bottlenecked by the exponentially growing number of Kraus operators with system size, rendering large-scale optimization prohibitive. While analytical near-optimal maps exist, they typically work only when the Knill-Laflamme conditions are nearly satisfied. In this Letter, we establish an efficient framework by leveraging the duality between recovery and environment decoupling. This framework yields a tighter analytical lower bound on entanglement fidelity than the conventional limit set by the transpose channel. Furthermore, by exploiting the decayed weights of noise Kraus operators, we introduce a framework based on principal component analysis to reduce the dimension. In thermal loss channels where the weights decay exponentially, our approach achieves a 33-fold computational speedup while maintaining rigorous accuracy. Our approach enables high-precision optimization for AQEC codes that were previously intractable due to the curse of dimensionality.
one_liner: An efficient AQEC optimization framework gives tighter fidelity bounds and faster recovery-channel computation.
why_it_matters: Reducing recovery optimization cost helps evaluate and design larger quantum error-correcting codes across hardware and bosonic platforms.
detailed_summary: The work reframes approximate quantum error correction through recovery-environment duality to derive tighter analytical lower bounds on entanglement fidelity. It also compresses the optimization by exploiting decaying Kraus-operator weights with a principal-component approach. For thermal loss channels, the method reports a 33-fold computational speedup while maintaining rigorous accuracy.
main_result: The paper demonstrates tighter fidelity certification and substantially faster optimization for AQEC codes with structured noise.
application_angle: This can make high-precision code benchmarking and recovery design practical for larger hardware-relevant noise models.

title: Invariant-based master equation applied to driven qutrit coupled to a bath and a leaky cavity
abstract: We employ a generalized approach to the master equation for driven open $N$-level ($N>2$) quantum systems using Lewis-Riesenfeld invariants, which avoids the driving-strength restrictions inherent to conventional approaches. We show that the invariant-based master equation provides a unifying generalized framework, which reduces to the frequently employed laboratory-frame master equations and the less frequently employed rotating-frame master equation framework under appropriate simplifications. Extending the prototypical two-level system, we show that the inclusion of another state coupled to the ground state via reservoir-induced dephasing gives rise to qualitatively new dissipative behaviors that are, in general, not captured by standard approximations. We also apply the invariant-based master equation framework to a driven quantum dot coupled to a leaky cavity, demonstrating the framework's ability to capture relevant dissipative dynamics without additional assumptions. Our work paves the way for quantum-control applications in the presence of dissipation.
one_liner: An invariant-based master equation captures driven multilevel dissipation beyond standard weak-driving approximations.
why_it_matters: More accurate open-system modeling can improve quantum control in driven qutrits, quantum dots, and cavity-coupled photonic devices.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a generalized master-equation approach for driven N-level open quantum systems using Lewis-Riesenfeld invariants. It recovers common laboratory- and rotating-frame equations under simplifying limits but avoids their usual driving-strength restrictions. Applying the method to a driven qutrit and a quantum dot coupled to a leaky cavity reveals dissipative effects missed by standard approximations.
platform_or_system: driven qutrit and quantum-dot cavity system
main_result: The invariant-based master equation provides a unified way to model driven multilevel dissipative dynamics without extra weak-driving assumptions.
application_angle: The framework supports more reliable pulse design and control analysis for photonic quantum emitters and cavity-QED devices.

title: A broadband, individually addressing two- and three-dimensional photonic integrated circuit for trapped-ion qubit control
abstract: Trapped ions provide a high-fidelity platform for quantum information processing, yet delivery of multiple, distinct wavelengths across large networks of interaction zones remains a bottleneck. Conventional free-space light delivery lacks scalability, while on-chip grating couplers suffer from narrow operational bandwidth that increases circuit footprint and optical interfacing complexity. Here we show a broadband photonic integrated circuit capable of addressing individual ions. The circuit combines a planar waveguide lens with a micromirror fabricated using two-photon polymerization at wafer scale. This implementation can address three individual ions from $λ$ = 405 - 880 nm with -27 dB average intensity crosstalk at $5\,μ\mathrm{m}$ pitch. We trap $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ and $^{138}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ ions above such devices, characterize optical crosstalk with barium ions, and demonstrate individual repumping of calcium ions. This monolithic photonic architecture brings broadband addressing in an on-chip modality to trapped-ion technology. More generally, integrating additive manufacturing into quantum devices is poised to unlock expanded design space for implementing novel quantum architectures.
one_liner: A broadband photonic integrated circuit individually addresses trapped ions from 405 to 880 nm with low crosstalk.
why_it_matters: On-chip broadband delivery tackles a major scaling bottleneck for trapped-ion processors that require many wavelengths and zones.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates a monolithic photonic integrated circuit for individual trapped-ion addressing over 405-880 nm. The architecture combines a planar waveguide lens with a two-photon-polymerized micromirror and reaches -27 dB average intensity crosstalk at 5 um ion pitch. The authors trap calcium and barium ions above the devices, characterize barium crosstalk, and show individual calcium repumping.
platform_or_system: integrated photonics for trapped Ca+ and Ba+ ions
main_result: The device delivers broadband, ion-resolved optical addressing in a chip-integrated architecture.
application_angle: It advances scalable trapped-ion control hardware by replacing bulky free-space optics and narrowband grating-coupler approaches.

title: Exceptional-point braiding with native controls
abstract: Exceptional points define branch-exchange state transfers through holomorphic continuation of non-Hermitian eigenmodes, but realizing these transfers dynamically remains difficult. Slow encircling does not generally transport the full set of instantaneous eigenstates, while shortcuts to adiabaticity can require controls outside the native experimental manifold. Here, we introduce a constrained shortcut-to-adiabaticity principle for exceptional-point braiding using native controls. In a dressed instantaneous-eigenstate frame, the available controls cancel the accessible transition channels locally, while the residual channels remain active during the evolution but are constrained to have no net accumulated effect over the closed loop. The protocol therefore targets the endpoint state transfer selected by ideal adiabatic branch exchange, rather than enforcing complete local cancellation or adiabatic following throughout the trajectory. We demonstrate the construction in a minimal two-mode non-Hermitian model equivalent, up to a trace shift and a basis convention, to the effective Hamiltonian used in dissipative-transmon exceptional-point experiments, where detuning and drive amplitude provide real controls and the relative loss imbalance fixes the non-Hermitian scale. Smooth real waveforms reshape only these controls, reproduce the branch-exchange transfer, and remain accurate under calibration errors, exceptional-point uncertainty and finite-bandwidth filtering with modest overhead.
one_liner: Native-control shortcuts enable robust exceptional-point braiding in a dissipative two-mode system.
why_it_matters: The protocol makes non-Hermitian state-transfer control more experimentally realistic for platforms such as dissipative transmons.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a constrained shortcut-to-adiabaticity method for exceptional-point braiding using only experimentally native controls. In a dressed instantaneous-eigenstate frame, accessible transition channels are locally cancelled while residual channels are constrained to have no net loop effect. A two-mode non-Hermitian model aligned with dissipative-transmon experiments shows robust branch-exchange transfer under calibration errors, exceptional-point uncertainty, and finite-bandwidth filtering.
main_result: Smooth real control waveforms reproduce exceptional-point branch-exchange state transfer without requiring non-native controls.
application_angle: This improves the feasibility of using non-Hermitian topology as a controllable resource in superconducting quantum hardware.

title: Agentic AI for Scientific Reasoning in Autonomous Quantum Sensing Experiments
abstract: We implement an agentic AI workflow built around a large language model (LLM) agent for autonomous experiments with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. NV centers are a widely used platform for quantum sensing, and the ability to control many measurements from a computer makes NV experiments a natural setting for autonomous workflows. We make two main contributions. First, we demonstrate an autonomous NV experiment workflow that combines persistent project records, quantitative calculation and data analysis tools, and deterministic experiment control. In one autonomous experiment, the agent selected a single NV center, calibrated its resonant frequency, measured \(T_2^\ast\) with Ramsey measurements, and added a Carr--Purcell--Meiboom--Gill (CPMG) measurement to check a weak feature that could be related to nearby \(^{13}\mathrm{C}\). Second, we introduce two offline benchmarks that evaluate the agent's reasoning separately from laboratory execution. We evaluated both benchmarks with GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol. In the Ramsey checkpoint benchmark, greater reasoning effort generally improved recognition of a residual resonance calibration offset. By contrast, in the pulsed optically detected magnetic resonance (pODMR) data evaluation benchmark, pulse sequence information alone produced more false positive resonance judgments at higher reasoning effort. Requiring an expected signal calculation kept false positive rates low across all three models and reasoning settings. The results suggest a clear division of labor for autonomous experiments. The agent forms scientific hypotheses and uses quantitative tools to evaluate data, while deterministic code controls the hardware and enforces safety constraints.
one_liner: An LLM-based agent autonomously runs NV-center sensing experiments while deterministic tools control hardware and safety.
why_it_matters: It shows how agentic AI can help plan, analyze, and adapt quantum sensing experiments without handing unsafe control to the model.
detailed_summary: The authors implement an agentic AI workflow for autonomous nitrogen-vacancy center experiments in diamond. In one run, the agent selected a single NV, calibrated resonance, measured T2* with Ramsey data, and added CPMG to probe a weak feature possibly related to nearby 13C. Offline benchmarks show that explicit expected-signal calculations reduce false positive resonance judgments across GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.6 Sol settings.
main_result: The system demonstrates autonomous NV experiment selection, calibration, measurement, and analysis with deterministic hardware control.
application_angle: The workflow is relevant for self-driving quantum sensors and labs where AI proposes hypotheses while verified code enforces execution constraints.

title: Exact Finite-Dimensional Evaluation of Homodyne Quantum Trajectories for Single-Quadrature Hamiltonian
abstract: Simulation of nonlinear stochastic master equations generally requires trajectory-level evolution of large Hilbert-space density matrices, making strongly nonlinear continuously monitored systems computationally challenging. Here we identify an exactly solvable class of continuously monitored systems consisting of polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, and homodyne measurement of the same quadrature. For Gaussian initial states, we derive an exact finite-dimensional stochastic representation of the conditional dynamics for arbitrary finite-order quadrature moments $\langle Q^mP^n\rangle$ through closure of the conditional momentum hierarchy. The resulting coefficient equations depend only on the Hamiltonian degree and moment order, with computational complexity $\mathcal{O}(C_{d,n}T)$, independent of the Hilbert-space dimension. The method requires no Fock-space truncation, Gaussian approximation, or moment closure approximation. Numerical simulations demonstrate agreement with direct stochastic master equation evolution and establish an efficient exact method for studying nonlinear homodyne trajectories in this class of continuously monitored systems.
one_liner: Exact finite-dimensional stochastic equations simulate nonlinear homodyne trajectories without Fock-space truncation.
why_it_matters: This gives a scalable exact simulator for a useful class of continuously monitored nonlinear photonic or oscillator systems.
detailed_summary: The paper identifies an exactly solvable class of continuously monitored systems with polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, and homodyne readout of the same quadrature. For Gaussian initial states, arbitrary finite-order conditional moments are represented by a closed finite-dimensional stochastic hierarchy. The resulting equations scale with Hamiltonian degree, moment order, and time, rather than Hilbert-space cutoff, and match direct stochastic master-equation simulations.
main_result: The authors derive and numerically validate exact finite-dimensional trajectory equations for polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians under homodyne measurement.
application_angle: The method can reduce simulation cost for designing and analyzing continuously measured nonlinear optical, microwave, or mechanical quantum devices.

title: Dissipation Enables Strongly Detuning-Dependent Interference in Pulsed Dynamical Decoupling
abstract: One of the defining features of pulsed dynamical decoupling is its suppression of a driven qubit's sensitivity to static detuning errors between the drive field and qubit resonance. In this paper, we show that dissipation, in the form of excited-state decay, can change this behavior entirely, producing an interference signal with a strong detuning dependence. This signal arises from decay during driven evolution and relies on coherence retained by the qubit after such a decay event. We develop analytical and numerical models that capture the underlying mechanism and observe this same dissipation-induced detuning dependence experimentally in both a free-space strontium atom interferometer and a superconducting transmon qubit system. We also use this dissipation-induced detuning dependence as the basis for a new spectroscopic technique called Dissipative Carr-Purcell Spectroscopy (DCPS) and compare it with a traditional Ramsey sequence. Our results establish a regime of pulsed dynamical decoupling in which dissipation reshapes, rather than merely degrades, coherent control, and we expect these dynamics to be relevant to a wide range of quantum systems.
one_liner: Decay turns pulsed dynamical decoupling into a strongly detuning-sensitive interferometer in atoms and transmons.
why_it_matters: It reframes dissipation as a usable control resource for spectroscopy, sensing, and hardware characterization rather than only an error channel.
detailed_summary: The work shows that excited-state decay during driven pulsed sequences can generate interference with strong detuning dependence, despite standard decoupling suppressing static detuning sensitivity. Analytical and numerical models attribute the effect to coherence retained after decay events during driven evolution. The effect is observed experimentally in a free-space strontium atom interferometer and in a superconducting transmon qubit, and is used to define Dissipative Carr-Purcell Spectroscopy.
platform_or_system: strontium atoms and superconducting transmon qubits
main_result: The authors demonstrate dissipation-induced detuning-sensitive interference and implement it as a new spectroscopy protocol, DCPS.
application_angle: DCPS offers a practical route to detuning spectroscopy and calibration in platforms where decay is unavoidable, including sensors and quantum processors.

title: Co-transmission of classical data and continuous-variable entanglement over a single quantum channel
abstract: Displacement-based simultaneous quantum-classical communications (SQCC) protocols, as originally proposed, are generally incompatible with the majority of useful quantum communication schemes, such as entanglement distribution or repeater-based quantum key distribution: direct measurement of the classical signal also measures and destroys the quantum state, leaving point-to-point Gaussian quantum key distribution as the only quantum communication scheme amenable to integration with SQCC. In this work, we apply the classically-modulated quantum communication protocol proposed by Zaunders and Ralph [arXiv:2606.03181v3] to circumvent this issue and demonstrate the distribution of continuous-variable Gaussian entanglement simultaneously with classical information. We characterise the quality of the distributed entangled state and outline how the scheme is suitable for use in repeater-based networks. Lastly, we compute the secret key generation rate of the Gaussian CMQC scheme in the point-to-point case and compare it to the equivalent point-to-point SQCC protocol.
one_liner: A modulated protocol distributes continuous-variable entanglement and classical data over the same quantum channel.
why_it_matters: It addresses quantum-classical coexistence without destroying the quantum state, a key requirement for integrated quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The paper applies a classically modulated quantum communication protocol to simultaneous transmission of classical information and continuous-variable Gaussian entanglement. Unlike displacement-based SQCC, the approach avoids direct classical readout that would measure and destroy the quantum state. The authors characterize the distributed entangled state, discuss repeater-network compatibility, and compare point-to-point Gaussian secret-key rates against conventional SQCC.
main_result: The authors show a scheme for co-transmitting classical data while preserving distributed continuous-variable Gaussian entanglement.
application_angle: The protocol could let quantum links share infrastructure with classical data channels while remaining compatible with entanglement distribution and repeater-based QKD.

title: Achieving 100$\,$MHz Instantaneous Bandwidth in a Broadband Rydberg Microwave Sensor
abstract: Rydberg atoms have attracted considerable attention in recent years as a novel platform for microwave sensing, owing to their unique physical merits: large transition dipole moments between Rydberg levels and broad frequency coverage. As a critical figure of merit for Rydberg microwave sensors, instantaneous bandwidth serves as a key benchmark for evaluating their viability in practical applications. Previous studies on instantaneous bandwidth remain limited to single-frequency operation, with typical demonstrated values of only tens of megahertz, a constraint that hampers the real-world deployment of this sensing technology. Here, we experimentally achieve an instantaneous bandwidth of over 100$\,$MHz across a broad frequency range of 2.7-20$\,$GHz and realize a sensitivity in the hundreds of nV$\,$cm$^{-1}\,$Hz$^{-1/2}$ range. The physical mechanism lies in the dressed-state coherence and the interference effect between different transition channels. Our work substantially broadens the instantaneous bandwidth of Rydberg microwave sensors and paves the way for their practical deployment in fields such as radar and wireless communications.
one_liner: A Rydberg microwave sensor reaches over 100 MHz instantaneous bandwidth from 2.7 to 20 GHz.
why_it_matters: Broad instantaneous bandwidth and nV/cm/Hz^1/2-level sensitivity move Rydberg receivers closer to practical RF sensing systems.
detailed_summary: The experiment demonstrates a broadband Rydberg-atom microwave sensor with instantaneous bandwidth exceeding 100 MHz across 2.7-20 GHz. The reported sensitivity is in the hundreds of nV cm^-1 Hz^-1/2 range. The authors attribute the broadband response to dressed-state coherence and interference between transition channels, extending prior single-frequency demonstrations limited to tens of MHz.
main_result: The main result is experimental realization of more than 100 MHz instantaneous bandwidth over a multi-GHz microwave range with high electric-field sensitivity.
application_angle: The performance targets requirements for deployable quantum RF receivers in radar, spectrum monitoring, and wireless communications.

title: Entanglement-based quantum key distribution with data in hollow-core fiber
abstract: The coexistence of quantum information and classical signals in a single fiber is essential for future quantum networks that leverage the well-established optical fiber infrastructure. Although multiplexing technologies can separate quantum and classical signals, pure silica core fibers (PSCFs) remain fundamentally limited by the high nonlinearity, which generates substantial Raman scattering and four-wave mixing noise. Hollow-core fibers (HCFs), guiding light predominantly in air, offer an attractive solution with intrinsically ultra-low nonlinearity and strongly suppressed nonlinear noise. In this work, we demonstrate the entanglement-based key coexisting with data over an 18-km HCF link. We achieve time-encoded high-dimensional quantum key distribution (HD-QKD) carrying 0 dBm of bidirectional received power, corresponding to a theoretical data capacity of up to 2.3 Tbps. During 24 hours of continuous operation, an average secret key rate (SKR) of 10.56 kbps is obtained. Theoretical analysis further predicts SKRs above 135 kbps over transmission distances exceeding 200 km using state-of-the-art low-loss HCFs. These results show significantly improved performance compared with PSCF-based systems and highlight the potential of HCFs for scalable quantum-classical coexistence compatible with the architectures of established fiber-optic networks.
one_liner: Entanglement-based HD-QKD coexists with bidirectional classical data over an 18 km hollow-core fiber.
why_it_matters: Hollow-core fiber suppresses nonlinear noise enough to support practical quantum-classical coexistence on telecom infrastructure.
detailed_summary: The paper demonstrates entanglement-based time-encoded high-dimensional QKD over an 18 km hollow-core fiber while carrying 0 dBm bidirectional received classical data power. The system runs continuously for 24 hours with an average secret key rate of 10.56 kbps. Modeling predicts more than 135 kbps beyond 200 km using state-of-the-art low-loss hollow-core fiber, benefiting from reduced Raman and four-wave-mixing noise compared with silica-core fiber.
main_result: The authors demonstrate stable entanglement-based HD-QKD coexisting with high-power bidirectional data in an 18 km hollow-core fiber link.
application_angle: This supports scalable deployment of quantum keys on data-bearing optical networks without requiring separate dark fiber.

title: Remote entanglement of massive oscillators via wire-mediated Coulomb interaction
abstract: We propose a method to enhance Coulomb interaction between charged macroscopic mechanical oscillators by placing a conducting structure in their vicinity. We derive the effective motional dynamics of the two oscillators using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics and show that image charges induced in the conductor fundamentally modify the range of the electrostatic interaction. For the specific case of a cylindrical wire, we predict that the coherent motional coupling changes from the free-space scaling $1/D^3$ to an asymptotic $1/(D\ln^2 D)$ dependence on the separation $D$ between the oscillators, at the cost of only negligible additional decoherence for low-frequency oscillators. We further show that, when combined with continuous position measurements, the enhanced interaction enables the generation of steady-state motional entanglement between the oscillators over significantly larger distances than achievable in free space. For experimentally realistic milligram-scale oscillators, we predict observable entanglement at separations of several hundred microns -- more than an order of magnitude beyond free-space capabilities -- with improvements approaching two orders of magnitude in future systems. These results identify conductor-assisted Coulomb interactions as a resource for quantum control of massive objects and for the exploration of entanglement generated by fundamental central forces.
one_liner: A conducting wire can extend Coulomb-mediated motional entanglement between massive charged oscillators.
why_it_matters: Conductor-assisted coupling could make table-top entanglement of macroscopic mechanical objects feasible over much larger separations.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes using a nearby conducting structure to enhance Coulomb coupling between charged macroscopic mechanical oscillators. Macroscopic QED modeling shows that image charges around a cylindrical wire change the interaction scaling from free-space 1/D^3 to asymptotic 1/(D ln^2 D), with negligible extra decoherence for low-frequency oscillators. Combined with continuous position measurements, the enhanced coupling is predicted to generate steady-state motional entanglement over separations of several hundred microns for realistic milligram-scale systems.
platform_or_system: charged macroscopic mechanical oscillators near a wire
main_result: The authors predict conductor-enhanced Coulomb coupling strong enough to generate remote steady-state motional entanglement beyond free-space limits.
application_angle: The scheme offers a hardware path for testing quantum control of massive objects and entanglement mediated by fundamental central forces.

title: Quantum teleportation over a field-deployed hollow-core fibre network
abstract: When a photon and one member of an entangled photon pair are jointly projected onto a Bell-state measurement (BSM), the quantum state of the photon can be transferred to the distant partner of the pair without physically transmitting this information carrier. In real-world deployment, however, teleportation performance is fundamentally bottlenecked by quantum channel impairments, such as loss, noise, and fluctuations, which induce severe decoherence and degrade fidelity. This vulnerability is further exacerbated in scenarios with intense classical data traffic or background light. Realizing scalable quantum networks, therefore, hinges on developing advanced channel architectures capable of supporting both high-fidelity quantum operations and high-capacity classical communications within a shared infrastructure. Towards this end, hollow core fibre (HCF) offers a promising quantum channel resource by combining free-space-like weak light-matter interaction with the stability of fibre-based systems. Here, utilizing a field-deployed metropolitan HCF network spanning three spatially separated nodes in Chengdu, we achieve quantum teleportation with an intermediate BSM under co-propagating classical traffic. Crucially, the HCF links preserve the long-term indistinguishability of photonic qubits without active stabilization, and exhibit a Raman noise approximately three orders of magnitude lower than that of standard solid-core counterparts. This noise suppression enables robust quantum teleportation even alongside classical launch powers up to 160 mW. Our findings establish a classical-data-compatible framework for quantum networking over deployed fibre infrastructure and offer a wavelength-agnostic, plug-and-play, and free-running pathway toward the quantum internet.
one_liner: Field-deployed hollow-core fibre links support quantum teleportation alongside high-power classical traffic.
why_it_matters: It shows a practical route for quantum networking over shared metro fibre while suppressing Raman noise and avoiding active stabilization.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates quantum teleportation across a three-node metropolitan hollow-core fibre network in Chengdu using an intermediate Bell-state measurement. The deployed HCF links maintain photonic-qubit indistinguishability over long times without active stabilization and show Raman noise about three orders of magnitude below solid-core fibre. Teleportation remains robust with co-propagating classical launch powers up to 160 mW, directly addressing coexistence with classical data traffic.
main_result: Quantum teleportation was achieved over deployed metropolitan HCF links while co-propagating intense classical traffic.
application_angle: The result supports plug-and-play quantum internet links that can share existing communication infrastructure with classical channels.

title: Quantum Teleportation toward the Quantum Internet: A Concise Review
abstract: Quantum networks play a pivotal role in quantum information science, which not only provide a secure communication platform for remote access to quantum computers but also serve as the strategic core for achieving large-scale quantum information processing, forming the foundational infrastructure for the future global-scale quantum internet. Quantum teleportation, which enables the transmission of unknown quantum states over long distances by employing quantum entanglement together with classical communication, is essential for the distribution of quantum resources in the construction of the global-scale quantum internet. To realize a global-scale quantum internet, quantum repeater protocols represent one of the most promising approaches for enabling quantum communication between any nodes. This concise review presents representative experimental demonstrations of quantum teleportation for constructing quantum networks across different physical platforms. Along this trajectory, the review discusses current challenges, open issues, and future perspectives toward scalable and practical quantum internet.
one_liner: A concise review surveys teleportation experiments and their role in building scalable quantum internet links.
why_it_matters: It organizes platform-level progress, repeater needs, and open issues for turning teleportation from lab demos into network infrastructure.
detailed_summary: This review summarizes representative experimental demonstrations of quantum teleportation across multiple physical platforms relevant to quantum networks. It frames teleportation as a core primitive for distributing unknown quantum states and quantum resources using entanglement plus classical communication. The paper also discusses quantum repeater protocols, scalability barriers, and practical challenges on the path to a global quantum internet.
main_result: The paper consolidates teleportation demonstrations and identifies the hardware and protocol gaps that remain for scalable quantum networking.
application_angle: It is useful as a compact roadmap for researchers planning quantum repeater, network-node, and interconnect development.

title: Repositories, Contributors, and Continuity: An Empirical Study of Foundational Quantum Software
abstract: Driven by contributions from academia, industry, and open-source communities, the quantum software ecosystem is rapidly growing. Across this ecosystem, new concepts often emerge through software artefacts accompanying scientific publications as well as through sustained development in larger communities. However, many repositories receive development efforts only over a limited period of time, raising the question whether their concepts persist beyond individual repositories. In this paper, we apply established empirical software engineering techniques to analyse a set of foundational quantum software repositories. We combine cross-repository activity with contributor relationships to study the evolution of communities. Our analysis provides empirical evidence of contributor migration patterns and indications of cross-project knowledge transfer. We observe multiple development paths: projects may evolve into sustained communities, contributors may integrate concepts into established ecosystems, or activity may continue through new and follow-up software artefacts. Our observations provide an initial empirical perspective on how concepts and influence persist across repository boundaries in quantum software ecosystems.
one_liner: An empirical study tracks how foundational quantum software projects and contributors evolve across repositories.
why_it_matters: Sustained quantum hardware and applications depend on reliable software ecosystems, not just isolated publication-linked code drops.
detailed_summary: The paper applies empirical software engineering methods to foundational quantum software repositories, combining cross-repository activity with contributor relationships. It identifies contributor migration patterns and evidence for knowledge transfer across projects. The analysis distinguishes multiple continuity paths, including sustained communities, absorption into established ecosystems, and follow-up artifacts after initial repositories become inactive.
main_result: The study provides empirical evidence that quantum software concepts can persist through contributor movement and cross-project development paths.
application_angle: The findings help hardware and application teams assess software sustainability risks when choosing quantum development stacks.

title: Quantum estimates for classical polynomial optimization
abstract: The problem of finding lower and upper bounds on multivariate homogeneous polynomials is both difficult and important given its applications to questions ranging from dynamical stability in complex potential landscapes to data analysis. From the standpoint of tensor eigenvalue theory, the question is equivalent to finding the smallest and the largest eigenvalues of the coefficient tensor corresponding to the given polynomial. Standard approaches outlined in the literature amount to running nonlinear iterations in search for the optimal rays along which the growth of the polynomial is fastest or slowest. Unlike the case of matrices (or their corresponding multivariate quadratic forms) convergence of such algorithms for higher-rank tensors is capricious due to the complex topography of polynomial objective functions. In this essay, a very different strategy, inspired by quantum-mechanical variational methods, is introduced for finding bounds on polynomials. The original polynomial is replaced by an operator acting in a suitably chosen (large) space of states, such that in an appropriate "classical" limit this operator approaches the original polynomial expression made of commutative variables. As a result, approximating the smallest and largest eigenvalues of the coefficient tensor, and thus finding bounds on polynomials, amounts to diagonalizing the resulting quantum operator, represented as a large matrix, and then inspecting the smallest and largest eigenvalues of this matrix. This approach is then successfully applied to standard test examples from tensor eigenvalue literature and other problems of interest in mathematical physics including Strichartz-type inequalities.
one_liner: A quantum-variational construction estimates bounds for classical homogeneous polynomial optimization problems.
why_it_matters: It imports operator diagonalization tools into hard tensor-eigenvalue problems with applications in mathematical physics and numerical analysis.
detailed_summary: The paper maps a classical homogeneous polynomial to an operator on a larger state space whose classical limit recovers the original commutative expression. Bounds on the polynomial are then estimated by diagonalizing the resulting large matrix and inspecting extremal eigenvalues. The method is tested on tensor-eigenvalue benchmarks and problems such as Strichartz-type inequalities, offering an alternative to unstable nonlinear iterations.
main_result: The main result is a diagonalization-based method for estimating lower and upper polynomial bounds through a quantum-mechanical operator construction.
application_angle: The approach could inform quantum-inspired algorithms and numerical tools for difficult optimization problems in physics and engineering.

title: Reconciling chemical models of X-ray Thomson Scattering with the Bethe $f$-sum rule
abstract: X-ray Thomson scattering (XRTS) is a key diagnostic for high-energy-density plasmas, which can exhibit significant quantum effects even at elevated temperatures. XRTS experiments are commonly interpreted using the Chihara decomposition, that was derived in the chemical picture and, thus, separates contributions from bound and free electrons. Despite being the de-facto standard for analysing measurements, a well-known shortcoming is that the standard bound-state treatment in the form of the impulse approximation fails to satisfy fundamental theoretical constraints, most notably the Bethe $f$-sum rule (BFSR). The problem arises due to the usage of plane waves in the impulse approximation as well as non-negligible contributions from bound-bound transitions. In this work, we present a minimal analytical extension of the Chihara decomposition of the dynamic structure factor for matter in the ground state, using hydrogenic bound-free and bound-bound transitions. We demonstrate that compliance with the BFSR is only achieved when both bound-bound transitions are explicitly included and an exact treatment of the bound-free contribution is applied. Finally, detector ray-tracing simulations for atomic hydrogen demonstrate experimentally detectable deviations from the standard Chihara model. The model will be made available in the open source XRTS library xDAVE [Bellenbaum et al., Phys. Plasmas (in print), arxiv:2604.27237].
one_liner: An extended XRTS model restores Bethe f-sum-rule consistency by treating bound-free and bound-bound transitions explicitly.
why_it_matters: More faithful XRTS interpretation improves diagnostics for high-energy-density plasmas where quantum electronic structure matters.
detailed_summary: The paper addresses a known inconsistency in standard Chihara-model analysis of X-ray Thomson scattering, where impulse-approximation bound-state treatments violate the Bethe f-sum rule. It adds an analytical hydrogenic treatment that includes exact bound-free contributions and explicit bound-bound transitions. Detector ray-tracing for atomic hydrogen predicts experimentally detectable deviations from the standard model, and the method is slated for the open-source xDAVE XRTS library.
main_result: The extended Chihara decomposition satisfies the Bethe f-sum rule only when exact bound-free and bound-bound terms are included.
application_angle: This can improve extraction of plasma properties from XRTS measurements in high-energy-density experiments.

title: Asymmetric information scrambling and eigenstate thermalization in inhomogeneous XXZ spin chains
abstract: Deterministic spatial inhomogeneity has become increasingly relevant in experimentally engineered quantum many-body systems, where interaction gradients can strongly influence nonequilibrium dynamics. Motivated by this, we investigate out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) and their connection to the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) in inhomogeneous XXZ spin chains. Using a deterministic spatially varying interaction profile, we show that finite interaction gradients ($δ>0$) induce a pronounced left--right asymmetry in information scrambling, as quantified by OTOCs. This asymmetry persists even when the system exhibits spectral signatures of quantum chaos, with operators on the strongly interacting side exhibiting suppressed scrambling. To elucidate the origin of the asymmetric finite-size long-time saturation value of OTOCs, we employ two complementary approaches. First, we analyze the diagonal matrix elements of the OTOC observables in the energy eigenbasis within the ETH framework. Second, we derive an analytical expression for the finite-size saturation value based on the overlap between the Hamiltonian and the OTOC observables, which explicitly incorporates the spatial interaction profile. The analytical prediction is fully consistent with the numerical results and provides a microscopic explanation for how deterministic interaction gradients generate the observed asymmetry in the long-time saturation of OTOCs.
one_liner: Inhomogeneous XXZ spin chains show direction-dependent information scrambling despite chaotic spectral signatures.
why_it_matters: Engineered interaction gradients can shape thermalization and operator spreading in controllable quantum simulators.
detailed_summary: The paper studies out-of-time-ordered correlators in XXZ spin chains with deterministic spatial interaction gradients. Numerical results show persistent left-right asymmetry in scrambling, with operators on the strongly interacting side scrambling less even when spectra indicate quantum chaos. The authors connect the finite-size OTOC saturation asymmetry to ETH matrix elements and derive an analytical expression based on overlap between the Hamiltonian and OTOC observables.
main_result: Finite interaction gradients generate asymmetric long-time OTOC saturation and direction-dependent scrambling in a chaotic spin chain.
application_angle: The result helps guide quantum-simulator designs where spatially engineered couplings are used to control transport, thermalization, or information flow.

title: Automated discovery of high-probability heralded schemes for path-entangled states
abstract: Entangled states of light lie at the heart of photonic quantum technologies, from distributed quantum communication to quantum-enhanced measurement and information processing. Their practical generation, however, remains constrained by the weak interactions between photons, which make the deterministic assembly of large multiphoton entangled states a central challenge in quantum optics. In this work, we use AI techniques to discover heralded linear-optical schemes for path-entangled states and show that the resulting solutions can be elevated from individual circuits to a new scalable family. This family contains previously known constructions as special cases while generally providing exponential and super-exponential improvements over those, and its extension to broader classes of target states shows how automated discovery can reveal transferable physical understanding. By presenting compact experimental proposals for large path-entangled states, our results provide both a theoretical advance in photonic heralding and a route towards a substantial leap in experimentally accessible multiphoton entanglement.
one_liner: AI-designed linear-optical circuits generate path-entangled photonic states with much higher heralding probabilities.
why_it_matters: Higher-probability heralded entanglement directly targets a bottleneck in scalable photonic quantum communication and multiphoton experiments.
detailed_summary: The paper uses AI methods to discover heralded linear-optical schemes for generating path-entangled states. The discovered circuits are generalized into a scalable family that includes known constructions but can give exponential or super-exponential success-probability improvements. The authors frame the results as compact experimental proposals for reaching larger multiphoton entangled states.
main_result: The work identifies a scalable family of heralded schemes for path-entangled states with substantially improved generation probabilities.
application_angle: Improved heralding rates could make larger photonic entangled resources more practical for quantum communication, metrology, and optical quantum processing.

title: Theory of Cubic-Phase Dynamics in the Linear Potential
abstract: A quantum wave packet in a linear potential, i.e., under a constant force such as gravity, accumulates a cubic-in-time phase that is universal across Schrodinger-type platforms and naturally realized by Airy eigenstates. Because the classical action is quadratic in the force, this phase comprises exactly three contributions: intrinsic, force-induced, and a cross term. The force-induced contribution alone is shape-independent, whereas the Airy eigenstate renders the shape-dependent contributions non-dispersing. An eigenstate-based nondimensionalization identifies the eigenforce, namely the intrinsic force underlying the packet's acceleration in the absence of an applied force, as a natural parameter. As a function of both forces, the cubic coefficient takes an analytically closed and physically interpretable form that factors along two zero lines: the static Airy eigenstate and a nontrivial zero at which the phase cancels without stationarity. This exposes the eigenforce as an effective antagonist to the applied force, not only in the caustic's self-acceleration but also within the phase, while leaving the centroid unaffected in accordance with Ehrenfest's theorem. Spatially uniform within each packet, the phase cannot be measured directly and is accessible only through the relative phase of two colliding packets, each evolving in its own potential. The general relative cubic coefficient, forbidden by symmetry for identical packets and activated by preparation asymmetry, therefore provides a designable signal. Extracted through heterodyne demodulation of the simulated interference between two Airy packets, its central value agrees with the prediction to sub-percent accuracy within the fitting uncertainty. The analysis spans ultracold-atom condensates, paraxial optics, and surface-gravity water waves.
one_liner: A theory predicts and numerically extracts cubic-in-time phases for Airy-like wave packets in linear potentials.
why_it_matters: It gives a controllable phase signal across optics, atoms, and wave systems that can be accessed through interferometric collisions.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes the cubic-in-time phase acquired by Schrodinger-type wave packets under a constant force and separates intrinsic, force-induced, and cross-term contributions. For Airy eigenstates, the shape-dependent terms remain non-dispersing, enabling closed-form design rules based on an eigenforce parameter. Simulated interference between two Airy packets recovers the predicted relative cubic coefficient with sub-percent agreement within fitting uncertainty.
platform_or_system: Airy wave packets in linear potentials
main_result: The main result is an analytic and numerically verified framework for engineering relative cubic phase signals between asymmetric wave packets.
application_angle: The phase-control framework is relevant to precision interferometry and wave-based sensing in paraxial optics, ultracold atoms, and water-wave analog systems.

title: Nonlocal Magnonic Cat States in Hybrid Magnon-Qubit Architectures
abstract: The quantum superpositions of coherent states offer an alternative to the conventional qubit-based encodings by harnessing the large Hilbert space available in bosonic modes, including those realised in microwave and optical cavities, magnons, and mechanical resonators. Beyond their advantages for local information processing, establishing long-distance quantum networks for such bosonic states is crucial for scalable quantum communication and distributed quantum computation. In this work, we propose an entanglement-swapping-based protocol to generate a bipartite magnonic cat state shared between spatially separated subsystems. Each subsystem comprises a hybrid architecture consisting of a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) sphere that supports magnon modes. By performing a projective Bell-state measurement on the qubits, the initially established magnon-qubit entanglement is coherently transferred to the remote magnon modes, resulting in a nonlocal magnonic cat state. For experimental characterisation of the gener- ated states, we perform quantum state tomography through reconstruction of the Wigner function using joint displaced parity measurements of the magnon modes. Our scheme provides a feasible route towards realising long-distance magnonic entanglement and contributes to the advancement of hybrid quantum network architectures.
one_liner: A protocol swaps qubit entanglement into remote YIG magnon modes to create nonlocal magnonic cat states.
why_it_matters: It connects bosonic cat-state encoding with distributed hybrid quantum networks using experimentally motivated magnon-qubit hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors propose two spatially separated hybrid subsystems, each combining a superconducting transmon qubit with a YIG sphere magnon mode. Local magnon-qubit entanglement is converted into remote magnon-magnon cat entanglement through a projective Bell-state measurement on the qubits. They also outline Wigner-function tomography using joint displaced parity measurements to characterize the generated state.
main_result: The work proposes an entanglement-swapping protocol for generating bipartite nonlocal magnonic cat states between remote hybrid nodes.
application_angle: Remote magnonic cat states could support distributed bosonic quantum information processing and hybrid quantum-network architectures.

title: KQFuzz: Knowledge-Guided Fuzzing for Quantum Libraries via Large Language Models
abstract: As quantum computing continually improves, ensuring the reliability and correctness of quantum libraries has become increasingly critical. To this end, many LLM-based fuzzing approaches towards quantum libraries have been proposed to uncover potential bugs. However, these methods still suffer from limitations such as insufficient flexibility and low efficiency, which hinder the progress of the quantum computing field. To address these challenges, we propose KQFuzz, a novel knowledge-guided fuzzer for quantum libraries. It leverages comprehensive codebase knowledge to ground LLM-based test generation, synergizing this with fitness-guided evaluation and two-level mutations to explore complex execution paths and trigger potential bugs. Firstly, KQFuzz introduces a novel prompting scheme tailored to quantum programs, which strategically incorporates knowledge of the codebase to efficiently generate high-quality quantum seed programs. Moreover, we develop evaluation and mutation strategies to handle the generated seed programs, facilitating efficient fuzzing execution while further enriching the diversity of the resulting test cases. We implement KQFuzz and conduct fuzzing on three popular quantum libraries, including Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, with coverage improved by up to 18.44%. During the development of KQFuzz, we discovered 13 bugs, all of which have been confirmed and 12 have already been fixed by the developers.
one_liner: KQFuzz uses codebase-aware LLM prompting plus guided mutation to find bugs in major quantum software libraries.
why_it_matters: Reliable quantum libraries are part of practical quantum hardware and algorithm deployment, and this method found confirmed real-world defects.
detailed_summary: KQFuzz grounds LLM-generated quantum test programs in codebase knowledge, then applies fitness-guided evaluation and two-level mutations to explore library behavior. It was evaluated on Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq, improving coverage by up to 18.44% over prior methods. The authors report 13 confirmed bugs discovered during development, with 12 already fixed by maintainers.
main_result: The system improves fuzzing coverage for quantum libraries and uncovers 13 confirmed bugs across widely used frameworks.
application_angle: Better automated testing reduces software failure risk in quantum application development, compilation workflows, and hardware-facing experiments.

title: Antichiral hinge states in a higher-order photonic nodal ring semimetal
abstract: Antichiral states propagate in the same direction on opposite boundaries, defying the conventional constraint that boundary modes must cancel net chirality. Previously found antichiral states have been limited to first-order topological semimetals. However, antichiral hinge states, the antichiral counterpart of recently discovered higher-order chiral hinge states, remain elusive. Here, we report the observation of antichiral hinge states in a higher-order nodal-ring semimetal made of a three-dimensional gyromagnetic photonic crystal. Near-field scanning measurements reveal a pair of hinge states at two parallel one-dimensional boundaries propagating unidirectionally along the same direction, with robust transport against metallic scatterers. Their spatial positions can be reconfigured by adding or removing photonic layers. The additionally observed antichiral and drumhead surface states manifest a hierarchy of first- and second-order topological boundary states within a single photonic system. Our work extends antichiral states to higher-order topological semimetals and has potential applications in robust and reconfigurable photonic routing.
one_liner: A 3D gyromagnetic photonic crystal shows reconfigurable antichiral hinge states with robust same-direction transport.
why_it_matters: It experimentally extends antichiral transport to higher-order photonic topology and points to robust reconfigurable routing.
detailed_summary: The paper reports antichiral hinge states in a higher-order nodal-ring semimetal implemented as a three-dimensional gyromagnetic photonic crystal. Near-field scanning observes unidirectional propagation in the same direction along two parallel hinges, including robustness against metallic scatterers. Adding or removing photonic layers reconfigures the hinge-state positions, while surface measurements reveal coexisting antichiral and drumhead boundary states.
main_result: The experiment observes reconfigurable higher-order antichiral hinge transport with robustness to metallic scattering.
application_angle: Such boundary modes could enable photonic interconnects and routers that are more robust and spatially reconfigurable than conventional waveguide layouts.

title: Counterfactual Quantum Sensing: What Interaction-Free Measurement Can and Cannot Buy
abstract: Interaction-free measurement infers the presence of an absorbing object from a photon that, in the counterfactual sense, never interacted with it, and is widely described as a route to minimally invasive sensing. We ask what it actually buys, in estimation-theoretic terms. Written as a channel-estimation problem, the Elitzur-Vaidman interferometer carries exactly half the Fisher information about the object's transmissivity that direct transmission probing does, and the two schemes deliver identical Fisher information per absorbed photon. For measuring how transparent something is, the interferometer buys nothing. The advantage lies in discrimination, and we show that what it requires is not that the object be opaque but that the competing hypothesis be the object's absence. Against empty space the Chernoff information per absorbed photon grows almost linearly, as the number of Zeno cycles times its logarithm, even for a weakly absorbing object; between two partial transparencies it does not grow at all. Parasitic loss in the cycle caps the advantage. The number of conclusive interrogations per absorbed photon reaches a maximum inversely proportional to the loss per cycle, at an optimal cycle number that is likewise inversely proportional to it, which identifies the loss per cycle as the figure of merit governing how far interaction-free sensing can be pushed. Finally, the negative result is not special to the interferometer. For a single photon meeting a memoryless, non-dispersive object any number of times through arbitrary fixed optics, the accessible quantum Fisher information never exceeds that of the same incident flux spent on independent single-pass probes, and is generically far below it. This recovers the bound of Massar, Mitchison and Pironio for this class, by a short argument that also identifies when it is tight.
one_liner: Counterfactual sensing is shown to help discrimination against absence, but not transmissivity estimation per absorbed photon.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when interaction-free measurement is practically useful and sets loss-driven limits for minimally invasive sensing.
detailed_summary: The paper recasts interaction-free measurement as a channel-estimation problem and compares it with direct transmission probing. For transmissivity estimation, the Elitzur-Vaidman interferometer carries half the Fisher information of direct probing and gives no advantage per absorbed photon. Its advantage appears in discrimination against empty space, where Chernoff information per absorbed photon can grow with Zeno cycling, but parasitic loss caps the gain. The authors further show a general single-photon bound for memoryless, non-dispersive objects under arbitrary fixed optics.
main_result: The main result is a set of estimation and discrimination bounds showing exactly what counterfactual sensing can and cannot improve.
application_angle: The analysis gives design criteria for low-damage optical sensing, identifying per-cycle loss as the key figure of merit.

title: Benchmarking Optical Receivers for Quantum Communication and Randomness Certification
abstract: The choice of optical receiver determines which properties of the transmitted states remain visible in the observed data and therefore affects the performance of different quantum protocols. We compare continuous-variable, photon-counting and hybrid receivers within the same prepare-and-measure framework, using semi-device-independent randomness generation as the main case study. The measurement device is left uncharacterised, while the source is described by the Gram matrix of its pure signal states using an energy-derived overlap constraint, a magnitude-Gram benchmark or the full complex Gram matrix of a certified coherent phase-shift-keyed constellation. Within this framework, the observed receiver statistics are used to bound $H_{\min}(B|X,Λ)$ against classical side information correlated with the measurement device but independent of the input. For a fixed Gram matrix, this bound is obtained from an exact semidefinite program, with complex multi-input cases treated in block-real form and checked through the corresponding dual certificate. Photon counting alone is phase blind for fixed-modulus phase encoding and therefore certifies no worst-case randomness. Continuous-variable receivers give the highest certified entropy at moderate energy, while under the nominal source calibration a hybrid receiver performs better at low energy when the beacon-region label is retained in the output. The same receiver statistics also provide receiver-level comparisons for discrete-modulated continuous-variable quantum key distribution, quantum reading, covert communication and quantum-signature verification, without replacing the full security analysis required for each protocol.
one_liner: Compares CV, photon-counting, and hybrid optical receivers for semi-device-independent randomness and quantum communication benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Receiver choice directly changes what protocol-relevant information survives measurement, affecting certified entropy and communication performance.
detailed_summary: The paper places continuous-variable, photon-counting, and hybrid optical receivers in a common prepare-and-measure benchmarking framework. Using source constraints from coherent-state Gram matrices, it bounds conditional min-entropy via exact semidefinite programs. The results show phase-blind photon counting fails for fixed-modulus phase encoding, while CV and hybrid receivers trade advantages across energy regimes.
main_result: It demonstrates receiver-dependent certified randomness bounds, with CV receivers strongest at moderate energy and hybrid receivers advantageous at low energy under nominal calibration.
application_angle: The framework helps choose receiver hardware for randomness generation, discrete-modulated CV-QKD, quantum reading, covert communication, and signature verification.

title: Time-Reversal Invariant Topological Photonic Alloy
abstract: Conventional approaches generate quantum spin Hall (QSH) and quantum valley Hall (QVH) effects by breaking spatial inversion symmetry across the entire photonic crystal. Consequently, modulating the bulk transmission gaps within these periodic frameworks typically requires global modification of structural parameters throughout the lattice, severely limiting device reconfigurability and post-fabrication adaptability. In this work, we demonstrate that global inversion symmetry breaking is not a prerequisite for inducing topological phases. Instead, local and minimal symmetry breaking is sufficient. Using a photonic alloy platform based on random substitutional disorder in a parallel-plate waveguide, we show that a disorder-driven local breaking of z-direction mirror symmetry and a local breaking of in-plane symmetry are capable of opening topological gaps to trigger QSH and QVH phase transitions, respectively, thereby supporting robust helical edge states and valley kink states. Rigorous topological characterization via the reflection-phase winding method reveals a striking size-dependent scaling behavior in both configurations, where the threshold doping concentration required to trigger the topological phase transition asymptotically vanishes in the thermodynamic limit. By enabling flexible, on-demand bulk gap engineering simply through random doping tuning rather than global structural reconfigurations, this photonic alloy platform not only deepens understanding of disorder induced topological physics but also offers a scalable, highly efficient design strategy for integrated topological optical communications.
one_liner: Shows disorder-tuned photonic alloys can induce QSH and QVH topological phases without global inversion-symmetry breaking.
why_it_matters: Random doping offers a post-fabrication route to engineer robust topological optical channels without redesigning the whole photonic crystal.
detailed_summary: The work uses a random substitutional photonic alloy in a parallel-plate waveguide to trigger topological phases through local symmetry breaking. Local z-mirror breaking opens QSH gaps, while local in-plane symmetry breaking opens QVH gaps. Reflection-phase winding analysis shows the critical doping concentration decreases with system size and vanishes asymptotically in the thermodynamic limit.
platform_or_system: randomly doped parallel-plate photonic waveguide alloy
main_result: It demonstrates disorder-driven topological gaps supporting helical edge states and valley kink states through tunable random substitution.
application_angle: This points to reconfigurable, scalable topological photonic components for robust integrated optical communication.

title: Lowering the implementation barrier of neutral-atom quantum computing with agentic workflows
abstract: Quantum computers are moving from research laboratories to industrial machines accessible via the cloud and integrated into high-performance computing facilities. However, translating theoretical quantum protocols into hardware experiments remains a major bottleneck, requiring expertise across protocol design, compilation, simulation, and cloud execution. Here, we introduce an agentic workflow that automates this pipeline on neutral-atom quantum processors (here two Pasqal QPUs available on the cloud) while keeping the researcher in the loop for critical validation. In three case studies from many-body physics and optimization, the agent went from published paper or patent to a QPU campaign run overnight. In particular, human intervention was crucial to ensure scientific validity: the agent selected an inadequate observable in one experiment and constructed a plausible but incorrect hardware diagnosis in another, with both failures detected only through domain-expert review.
